nodes.description:
The initiating lesion. Reported alleles span the mutational spectrum a loss-of-function gene would be expected to show: a start-codon-destroying variant paired with a missense in the index patient, a homozygous missense in the second, and a homozygous in-frame single-residue deletion p.(A78del) plus a homozygous missense p.(R337C) in the optic-atrophy families.
Structural modelling in the 2026 series places two of these residues in the subunit's protein-protein interfaces rather than in any catalytic site, which is what an accessory-subunit lesion should look like: the variant degrades the subunit's ability to hold on to its neighbours, not its ability to turn over substrate.

nodes.description:
The severe pole. Leigh syndrome is a pathological diagnosis as much as a clinical one - bilateral, symmetric spongiform degeneration of the basal ganglia, brainstem, thalamus, cerebellum, spinal cord and optic nerves - and isolated complex I deficiency is its commonest biochemical cause. Two NDUFA10 patients have carried that diagnosis, and the gene appears among the nuclear Leigh genes of a 219-patient Russian cohort.
Marked PROVISIONAL rather than ESTABLISHED because the association between NDUFA10 loss and this lesion distribution rests on a small number of patients diagnosed clinically and radiologically; no NDUFA10 case has been examined neuropathologically, and why complex I deficiency selects these structures is not answered by any source cited here. The edge into this node is typed with unknown intermediates for the same reason: the steps between a cell-level bioenergetic deficit and a stereotyped lesion distribution are exactly what is missing.

nodes.description:
Reported in one of the two NDUFA10 families in the 2026 optic-atrophy series. The attribution needs its reasoning stated, because the quoted sentence names two families without naming their genes: cerebellar atrophy was found in Families J and L, and the same paper assigns Family J to NDUFA1 and Families K and L to the homozygous NDUFA10 p.(A78del) allele. So Family L is the NDUFA10 case and Family J is not. That is a structural inference across two passages of one paper rather than a single quotable statement, which is why the evidence below is marked INDIRECT and why the reasoning is written out here rather than left for the reader to reconstruct.
One patient, so no frequency band. It is worth curating because it is the only structural neuroimaging finding attributed to an NDUFA10 patient anywhere in the citable literature, and because cerebellar atrophy sits outside the optic nerve - evidence that even the mild pole of this entity is not always confined to the visual pathway.

This is the step that distinguishes an accessory-subunit disease from a core-subunit one: a defective core subunit would be expected to leave a normal or near-normal amount of assembled enzyme with reduced turnover, whereas losing the scaffolding subunit costs the enzyme itself.

nodes.description:
Curated as a clinical diagnosis rather than decomposed into HPO signs, because that is the granularity at which the sources report it. HPO has no term for Leigh syndrome - it is a disease concept, held in MONDO and OMIM - so `phenotype_term` carries a free-text `preferred_term` with no binding, rather than a substituted approximation such as an abnormal-basal-ganglia term, which would assert an imaging finding not reported per patient here.
Two patients carry the diagnosis in the primary reports, and NDUFA10 also appears among the nuclear genes solved in a 219-patient Russian Leigh cohort - a third, unquantified ascertainment.
A published third case exists and is not curated as evidence. PMID:36270260 is a letter titled "Juvenile-onset dystonia with spasticity in Leigh syndrome caused by a novel NDUFA10 variant"; it has no abstract, and neither PubMed nor its DOI returns any body text, so its cached record is empty. Its title is the only accessible statement about it, and a title is not a finding. Dystonia and spasticity are therefore NOT curated as phenotypes of this entity, and the juvenile onset it reports is not curated either.

nodes.description:
A regulatory function of NDUFA10 discovered from the other end - not by studying NDUFA10 disease, but by asking why PINK1 loss reduces complex I activity. Phosphoproteomics of complex I in Pink1-null mouse liver and brain found a specific loss of phosphorylation at NdufA10 serine-250, and that phosphorylation turned out to be required for ubiquinone reduction by the complex.
The claim is contested, and the contradiction is curated below rather than smoothed over. An independent Drosophila study reached the opposite conclusion about the site itself: overexpressing ND42, the fly NDUFA10 homologue, did restore complex I activity and partially rescue locomotion in pink1 mutants, but that rescue showed no specific requirement for phosphorylation at Ser-250. So the two studies agree that NDUFA10 abundance governs complex I activity downstream of PINK1, and disagree about whether the serine-250 phospho-switch is the mechanism.
Whether any of this bears on MC1DN22 is a separate and unexamined question. No phosphorylation measurement has been made in an NDUFA10 patient's cells, and none of the alleles quotable here is described as affecting serine-250. The node is curated as a hypothesis about a second, potentially separable arm of the lesion, and its edge to the measured endpoint is typed as having unknown intermediates for that reason.
nodes.id: Loss of Serine-250 Control of Ubiquinone Reduction

nodes.description: The functional consequence common to every reported allele: complex I is built without a working copy of NDUFA10. What follows depends on what the subunit is for, and here the literature is unusually blunt - beyond stabilising the complex I holoenzyme, no specific function has been described for it. That is the ordinary reading of the disease, and the two hypothetical nodes below are the two candidate exceptions to it.

nodes.description:
A second property of NDUFA10 that has no counterpart in most complex I accessory subunits, and whose relevance to this disease is unknown. NDUFA10 retains a deoxyribonucleoside-kinase fold, and the large majority of the dGTP inside mitochondria is bound to it - tightly enough to survive mitochondrial isolation and methanol treatment. Engineering the dNK domain in HEK-293T cells, while deliberately preserving complex I assembly and activity, halves mitochondrial dGTP content. The authors propose the interaction as a link between oxidative metabolism and mitochondrial DNA maintenance.
Marked HYPOTHETICAL, and it is worth being precise about what is hypothetical. That NDUFA10 holds most mitochondrial dGTP is measured, not conjectured. What is conjectural is that this matters in MC1DN22: no patient allele has been tested for dGTP binding, no mitochondrial DNA depletion or deletion phenotype has been reported in an NDUFA10 patient, and the experiment that isolates the dGTP function used a mutant chosen precisely because it does *not* destabilise the complex - the opposite of what the disease alleles do. The node is curated because it is a testable prediction unique to this gene, not because there is evidence for it.

nodes.description: The presentation of the 2026 cohort, and in two siblings the entire disease. Recorded without a frequency band on purpose: the cohort was ascertained by starting from patients who already had optic atrophy, so its share of NDUFA10 patients tells you about the screen's design rather than about the disease. What the same series does establish is a genuine phenotypic discordance within a single allele - two siblings homozygous for p.(R337C) had isolated optic atrophy, while a previously published patient with the same amino-acid change had multisystem disease.

nodes.description:
The mild pole, and the reason this entity is not simply "NDUFA10 Leigh syndrome". A 2026 screen of complex I genes in patients with optic atrophy found biallelic NDUFA10 variants in three families and reported optic atrophy - isolated in one of them - as a presentation of this gene for the first time. The optic nerve is not a surprising target: it is already on the list of structures degenerating in Leigh syndrome, and retinal ganglion cells are the classic casualty of complex I failure in the mitochondrial optic neuropathies.
PROVISIONAL because the number of families is small, because the series is a targeted ascertainment of patients who already had optic atrophy - so it cannot say how often NDUFA10 disease presents this way - and because no mechanism specific to retinal ganglion cells has been demonstrated for this gene.

evidence.snippet: Furthermore, isolated or plus OA was found for the first time in NDUFV2, NDUFA1, NDUFA10 and NDUFAF3 families, for which only a single report of arLHON existed for a patient carrying NDUFA10 variants.

nodes.description:
The measured endpoint, and the best-evidenced claim in this entry. Both the amount and the activity of complex I fall, in fibroblasts and in muscle tissue, and the two falling together is the signature of an assembly or stability defect rather than a catalytic one.
Conformance note: the module pairs decreased oxidative phosphorylation with increased reactive oxygen species. Only the first arm is evidenced here - reactive oxygen species have not been measured in an NDUFA10 patient and are not asserted. The module's upstream node, age-related mitochondrial damage and mtDNA mutation, does not apply to a primary nuclear subunit defect, so conformance is declared at this node alone.
